cards.title: Seema Misra
cards.prompt: A subpostmistress ran "the computer did it" as her defence in front of a jury. Name her, and say what the verdict cost her.
cards.body: Seema Misra — an SPM, the judgment's word for subpostmaster — ran the West Byfleet branch. Charged with theft and false accounting over about £74,000, she blamed Horizon. A jury convicted her at Guildford Crown Court in late 2010; she was sentenced to 15 months, pregnant at the time. Fujitsu's Gareth Jenkins gave expert evidence for the prosecution.
cards.answer: Seema Misra, West Byfleet: convicted by a jury in late 2010 over about £74,000 and jailed for 15 months while pregnant, with Fujitsu's expert testifying against her.

cards.title: The Dalmellington bug
cards.prompt: One scan of a cash pouch, four entries in the branch accounts. What made the terminal repeat itself, and how long did the defect run before anyone named it?
cards.body: A log-on script left on the stack of incomplete processes made the pouch-delivery script believe it had not finished, so it repeated its last part — writing duplicate remittances under duplicate pouch IDs. Fraser J found its effects ran 2010 to 2015: over 110 occurrences, probably 116, across 88 branches. It is named for the branch that finally noticed.
cards.answer: An unclosed log-on script left the pouch-delivery script thinking it was unfinished, so it repeated the remittance; the effects ran 2010–2015 across 88 branches before it was named.

cards.title: The Callendar Square bug
cards.prompt: Before Dalmellington came a bug that made committed transactions vanish from the counter. Name the branch it is named after, and say what Fujitsu's own support note told staff to warn postmasters against.
cards.body: Also called the Falkirk bug. Riposte hit an error while inserting a message, replication stalled, and transactions disappeared from the counter. Staff re-keyed them; transfers then doubled up and the office balanced £6,414.46 short. Fujitsu's support note carried the workaround: warn the postmaster that apparently missing transactions "should not be re-entered".
cards.answer: Callendar Square, Falkirk, 2005 — and Fujitsu's note told staff to warn postmasters not to re-enter transactions that appear missing, because they reappear after a reboot.

cards.title: Bates & Others v Post Office Ltd (No. 6), "Horizon Issues"
cards.prompt: You can open a judge's paragraph-by-paragraph schedule of one production system's bugs. Which judgment is it, who wrote it, and what did it find about the risk to branch accounts?
cards.body: Mr Justice Fraser's sixth judgment in the Post Office Group Litigation, handed down 16 December 2019, with a Technical Appendix that works through the agreed Bug Table one defect at a time. Its finding: there was "a significant and material risk" of branch accounts being affected by bugs, errors and defects.
cards.answer: Bates & Others v Post Office Ltd (No. 6), the Horizon Issues judgment of Fraser J, [2019] EWHC 3408 (QB), 16 December 2019; it found a significant and material risk that bugs affected branch accounts.

cards.title: Convictions quashed by statute
cards.sub: 2024 · UK Parliament and the Scottish Parliament
cards.prompt: Overturning these convictions one appeal at a time could not keep up with the volume. What did the legislatures do instead in 2024?
cards.body: They quashed the convictions wholesale. The Post Office (Horizon System) Offences Act 2024 covered England, Wales and Northern Ireland; the Post Office (Horizon System) Offences (Scotland) Act 2024 covered Scotland. Both exonerated by statute rather than case by case, routing claimants into a new Horizon Conviction Redress Scheme. Verdicts reversed in bulk, because the evidence was a computer's word.
cards.answer: Two 2024 Acts — one for England, Wales and Northern Ireland, one for Scotland — quashed Horizon convictions by statute instead of appeal by appeal, feeding claimants into the Horizon Conviction Redress Scheme.

cards.title: Paying back money that never went missing
cards.prompt: Most of the people hit by Horizon were never prosecuted — they just made the shortfall good out of their own pockets. Roughly what had the scheme for them paid out by spring 2025, on how many claims?
cards.body: The Horizon Shortfall Scheme covers postmasters who repaid phantom shortfalls. As at 30 April 2025 it had taken 9,437 eligible claims, made 6,644 offers, and paid out £507m in full and final awards and interim payments. It is one of four separate redress schemes, and not the one for quashed convictions.
cards.answer: £507m paid out on 9,437 eligible claims as at 30 April 2025 — and the Horizon Shortfall Scheme was only one of four redress schemes.
